'''Dame Anne Laura Dorinthea McLaren''', {{postnominals|country=GBR|sep=,|DBE|FRS|FRCOG}} (26 April 1927&nbsp;– 7 July 2007)<ref name="ODNB">{{cite ODNB |last1=May |first1=Alex |title=McLaren, Dame Anne Laura Dorinthea (1927–2007), geneticist |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-98949 |access-date=26 April 2021 |language=en |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/98949 |date=6 January 2011|isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 }}</ref> was a British scientist who was a leading figure in [[developmental biology]].<ref name=anne>{{cite journal|title=An Interview with Anne McLaren|journal=Nature Reviews Genetics|volume=8|issue=6|year=2007|pages=412|issn=1471-0056|doi=10.1038/nrg2123|pmid=17571324|first=Magda|last=Skipper|author-link=Magdalena Skipper|doi-access=free}}</ref> She paved the way for women in science and her work helped lead to human [[in vitro fertilisation]] (IVF).<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Anne Laura Dorinthea McLaren (1927-2007) {{!}} Embryo Project Encyclopedia |url=https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/anne-laura-dorinthea-mclaren-1927-2007 |access-date=2023-11-24 |website=embryo.asu.edu}}</ref> She left an enduring legacy marked by her research and ethical contributions to the field. She received many honours for her contributions to science, including election as fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name=":1" />

==Early life==
McLaren was born into a privileged family with notable lineage, as the fourth of five children.<ref name=":0" /> She was the daughter of Sir [[Henry McLaren, 2nd Baron Aberconway]], a former [[Liberal Party (UK)|Liberal]] MP, and Christabel Mary Melville MacNaghten. She was born in London and spent her early childhood there, attending private schools.<ref name="Regen Med Obit" /> At the age of seven she appeared in the film version of [[H. G. Wells]]' novel ''[[Things to Come]]'', released in 1936.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{IMDb name|id=0572196}}</ref> At the outbreak of World War II, she was 12 years old and her family moved to their estate at [[Bodnant Garden|Bodnant]], North Wales.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Regen Med Obit" /> During this time her education was interrupted, so she pursued solitary education through a [[correspondence course]]. She enjoyed writing mathematical puzzles, arithmetic, books, and educational pamphlets. At the age of 16 she returned to formal education and attended a private school at [[Longstowe]] Hall near [[Cambridge]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1945, she was awarded a scholarship for the next year at [[Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford]].<ref name=":0" /> Her first two years were spent studying [[Honour Moderations|Honours Moderations]] in zoology, physics and mathematics, and her next two years were spent pursuing a course of study in [[zoology]]. She earned a Master of Arts ([[Master of Arts (Oxbridge)|MA]]) in 1949. She continued her post-graduate studies at [[University College London]] from 1949: researching mite infestation of ''[[Drosophila]]'' under [[J. B. S. Haldane|J.B.S. Haldane]], she became the first women to win a Christopher Welch Scholarship.<ref name=":0" /> She obtained her Doctor of Philosophy in 1952 with [[Peter Medawar]] on the genetics of rabbits, and then on neurotropic murine viruses under Kingsley Sanders.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Aucott |first=Rachel |date=2019-03-20 |title=Dame Anne McLaren |url=https://www.zoo.cam.ac.uk/alumni/biographies-of-zoologists/dame-anne-mclaren |access-date=2023-11-23 |website=www.zoo.cam.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>

==Married life and early career==
On 6 October 1952, she married fellow student [[Donald Michie]].<ref name=":1" /> They worked together at [[University College London]] from 1952 to 1955, and afterwards at the [[Royal Veterinary College]], on the variation in the number of [[lumbar vertebrae]] in mice as a function of maternal environment. McLaren would later take up research on fertility in mice, including [[Controlled ovarian hyperstimulation|superovulation]] and [[superpregnancy]].<ref name="Christs">{{cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = J | year = 2007 | title = Prof. Dame Anne McLaren DBE, FRS (Fellow-Commoner 1991) | journal = Christ's College Magazine | volume = 232 | pages = 112–114 }}</ref> In 1958, she published a landmark [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']] paper with [[John D. Biggers]] reporting the first successful development and birth of mice embryos that were first recovered from naturally fertilized females at the 8–16 cells stage, then cultured in vitro for two days until the [[blastocyst]] stage, and finally transferred back to females' uterus until birth.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=McLaren|first=Anne|date=1958|title=Successful Development and Birth of Mice cultivated in vitro|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/182877a0#citeas|journal=Nature|volume=182|issue=4639|pages=877–878|doi=10.1038/182877a0|pmid=13590153|s2cid=4217944|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This paper, "Successful Development and Birth of Mice cultivated in vitro as Early Embryos", has been called "one of the most significant papers in the history of reproductive biology and medicine".<ref name=stfobituary>{{cite news |last=Leese |first=Henry |title= In Memoriam Professor John Biggers |url= http://srf-reproduction.org/who-we-are/in-memoriam/|work= Society for Reproduction and Fertility|date= 7 April 2018|access-date= 6 August 2018}}</ref> This was a highly productive time in her life and she contributed to 28 papers.<ref name=":0" />

During this period, she had three children:

* [[Susan Michie]] (1955)<ref name="Regen Med Obit" />
* [[Jonathan Michie]] (1957)<ref name="Regen Med Obit" />
* Caroline Michie (1959)<ref name="Regen Med Obit" />

The marriage ended in divorce in 1959, and McLaren moved to the [[Roslin Institute|Institute of Animal Genetics]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]] to continue her research. The couple remained on good terms; Michie also moved to Edinburgh. The experience of raising children as a single career parent made McLaren a strong advocate for government assistance towards childcare.<ref name="Christs"/><ref name="Regen Med Obit"/>

==Later career==
McLaren spent the next 15 years (1959–1974) at the Institute of Animal Genetics, studying fertility, development and epigenetics, including the development of mouse [[Embryo transfer|embryonic transfer]], [[immunocontraception]], and the skeletal characteristics of [[Chimera (genetics)|chimerae]].<ref name="Christs"/><ref name="Regen Med Obit"/> She published a highly renowned book on Chimaeras in 1976,<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Anne McLaren |url=https://www.gurdon.cam.ac.uk/about-us/our-history/anne-mclaren/ |access-date=2023-11-24 |website=Gurdon Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> receiving her first major award that same year. The [[Zoological Society of London]]'s Scientific Medal, recognized her leading role in developing techniques for [[blastocyst transfer]] into recipient mice.<ref name="Regen Med Obit" />

In 1974, she left Edinburgh to become the Director of the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|MRC]] Mammalian Development Unit in London.<ref name=":0" /> She held this position for 18 years.<ref name=":0" /> During this time she collaborated with Marilyn Monk, who played a significant role in Anne's research on germ cells.<ref name=":0" />  She also contributed to teaching and lecturing and took on leadership roles in scientific societies.<ref name=":0" />

McLaren's work often took her outside the university. She was a member of the committee established to inquire into the technologies of in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and embryology, which later produced the [[Warnock Report]]. She was a member of the [[Nuffield Council on Bioethics]], 1991–2000.<ref name=":0" />

In 1992, she retired from the Unit and moved to [[Cambridge]] where she worked for the next 15 years.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Christs" /> She joined the Wellcome/CRC Institute, later the [[Gurdon Institute]]. She was made a Fellow-Commoner of [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] in 1991.<ref name="Christs" /> During this period she pursued her interests in sex determination, germ cells, and genomic imprinting, contributing to 48 papers.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> In addition, she used her position to promote women in academia and became an Honorary Fellow of [[Lucy Cavendish College, Cambridge|Lucy Cavendish College]] in 1994.<ref name=":0" /> She was active in her support in the advancement of women in science and was a founder of the Association of Women in Science and Engineering (AWiSE). She was president of the AWiSE for several years.<ref name="Regen Med Obit" />

In 2004, McLaren was one of the co-founders of the [[Frozen Ark]] project, along with husband and wife [[Bryan Clarke|Bryan]] and [[Ann Clarke (immunologist)|Ann Clarke]]. The project's aim is "saving the DNA and viable cells of the world's endangered species".<ref name="frozen">{{cite web |title=Information about the Frozen Ark |url=https://www.frozenark.org/the-frozen-ark/ |publisher=The Frozen Ark Project |access-date=9 February 2020 |archive-date=12 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191112171448/https://www.frozenark.org/the-frozen-ark/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Research ==
While obtaining her doctorate in philosophy, she investigated the mechanisms of virus infection on the nervous system.<ref name=":1" />

After her doctoral work, she shifted her research to embryology (now called [[developmental biology]]). With [[Donald Michie]], she conducted joint research on the influence of maternal environment on lumbar vertebral counts in mice and gained expertise in the manipulation of mouse embryos.<ref name=":2" /> This research demonstrated the feasibility of cultivating mouse embryos in a lab setting and successfully achieving live births by implanting them into the uterus of a surrogate mother.<ref name=":2" />  In 1958, in collaboration with [[John D. Biggers]], she published a seminal paper on the successful development and birth of mice cultivated [[In vitro fertilisation|in vitro]]. They showed successful birth after experimenting on embryos and blastocysts directly from one mother to another. These techniques became the basis for [[IVF]].<ref name=":3" />

During her collaborative research with Marilyn Monk and [[Elizabeth Simpson (biologist)|Elizabeth Simpson]] on [[Sex assignment|sex determination]] and male fertility, she identified the earliest [[primordial germ cells]] through alkaline phosphatase staining and explored the role of [[Testis cord|testes cord]] formation and [[meiosis]] blockage in male [[genital ridge]]s.<ref name=":0" />

She contributed to regenerative medicine by exploring the [[pluripotency]] of mammalian embryos and its therapeutic implications.<ref name=":0" />

== Honours and awards ==
In 1975, McLaren was made a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Clarke |first1=Ann |last2=Johnson |first2=Martin H. |date=2023 |title=Anne Laura Dorinthea McLaren DBE. 26 April 1927 — 7 July 2007 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.2022.0053 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=74|pages=309–337 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0053 |s2cid=257233529 |url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref> From 1991 to 1996, she held the position of Foreign Secretary of the Royal Society and from 1992 to 1996 the position of vice-president; she was the first female officer in the society's 330-year history.<ref name=":2" /> In 1986, she was made a Fellow of the [[Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists]] for her pioneering work on fertility.  In 1989 she presented the [[Ellison-Cliffe Lecture]] at the [[Royal Society of Medicine]], and from 1990 to 1995 she was the [[Fullerian Professor of Physiology]] at the [[Royal Institution]].

In 1993, she was created a [[Order of the British Empire|DBE]]. From 1993 to 1994, she was president of the [[British Association for the Advancement of Science]], and in 1998 she was made a Fellow of the [[Academy of Medical Sciences (United Kingdom)|Academy of Medical Sciences]].<ref name="Regen Med Obit">{{cite journal|last1=Franklin|first1=Sarah|title=Obituary: Dame Dr Anne McLaren|journal=Regenerative Medicine|year=2007|volume=2|issue=5|pages=853–9|doi=10.2217/17460751.2.5.853|pmid=17907937}}</ref>

In 2001, she was awarded the Lifetime Achievement Award from the [[Society for Developmental Biology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Society for Developmental Biology {{!}} Society for Developmental Biology Lifetime Achievement Award |url=https://www.sdbonline.org/lifetime_achievement_award |access-date=2026-06-03 |website=www.sdbonline.org |language=en}}</ref> In 2002, she was the only female recipient awarded the [[Japan Prize]] with [[Andrzej K. Tarkowski]] for their contributions to developmental biology.<ref name=":1" /> In 2007 she was awarded the [[March of Dimes Prize in Developmental Biology]].<ref name=":1" />

==Death==
After reuniting in 2005, McLaren (aged 80) and Michie (aged 83) were killed on 7 July 2007, in a car accident on the [[M11 motorway]] as they travelled from Cambridge to London.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="bbcobit">{{Cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/6281348.stm|title=Academic pair killed in car crash|work=[[BBC News]]|date=8 July 2007|access-date=5 April 2016}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
Anne McLaren's collaboration with Marilyn Monk and [[Elizabeth Simpson (biologist)|Elizabeth Simpson]] significantly advanced our modern understanding of sex determination and male fertility.

Her book "Mammalian Chimeras," published in 1976, solidified her as one of the world's leading experts in chimeras.<ref name=":0" /> She also published a book titled ''Germ Cells and Soma'' in 1967. Both of these are considered classics in the field.<ref name=":2" />

In addition to her research, she played an important role in addressing the social, ethical, and political dimensions of [[cloning]] and [[stem cell]] research by actively engaging in bioethical discussions and contributing to the understanding of the implications of these technologies. Her involvement in discussions and her commitment to considering the broader social impact of these advancements marked her as a prominent voice surrounding these groundbreaking technologies.<ref name="Regen Med Obit" />

She is remembered for her participation in setting up the Stem Cell Centre and the Centre for Trophoblast Research at [[Cambridge University]].<ref name=":0" /> A biographical sketch published by the university's Department of Zoology describes her as one of the most distinguished practitioners of [[developmental biology]].<ref name=":1" />

The Anne McLaren Papers are housed at the [[British Library]] and can be accessed through the British Library catalogue.<ref>[http://searcharchives.bl.uk/IAMS_VU2:IAMS032-001977955 Anne McLaren Papers], archives and manuscripts catalogue, the British Library. Retrieved 15 May 2020</ref>

There is a fund in the name of Anne McLaren for encouragement of scientific study.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite web|title=The Anne McLaren Memorial Fund|url=http://www.christs.cam.ac.uk/default/events/anne-mclaren-memorial-fund|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303235641/http://www.christs.cam.ac.uk/default/events/anne-mclaren-memorial-fund|archive-date=3 March 2016|access-date=25 July 2013|publisher=Christ's College Cambridge}}</ref> Cambridge University's Anne McLaren Laboratory for Regenerative Medicine was opened at the [[Cambridge Biomedical Campus]] in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2 June 2009|title=New centre for biomedical research opens|url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/news/new-centre-for-biomedical-research-opens|access-date=23 August 2020|website=[[University of Cambridge]]|language=en}}</ref>

On 26 April 2021, [[Google]] celebrated her 94th birthday with a [[Google Doodle]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://doodles.google/doodle/anne-mclarens-94th-birthday/ |title=Anne McLaren's 94th Birthday |website=Google |date=26 April 2021 }}</ref>

There is an Anne McLaren Award for scientific excellence and associated lecture at [[Kellogg College]] Oxford. The college also has a guest accommodation building named in her honour.<ref>{{cite web |title=Awards |website=Kellogg College |date=2025-06-17 |url=https://www.kellogg.ox.ac.uk/study/awards/ |access-date=2025-08-29}}</ref>
